opus-5.5.text:
Part of it is just that I think nobody, including me, including the labs, including any government agency, actually knows how this is going to go. We're in a situation of deep uncertainty about how quickly capabilities will advance, what the warning signs of danger will look like, and what the right policy responses are. When you're that uncertain, the thing you most want is for as many smart, differently-situated people as possible to be looking at the evidence and arguing about it.

If you funnel everything through a small government body, you're betting that this one group of people will have the right expertise, the right incentives, and enough independence from the companies they're overseeing to interpret the information correctly. That's a big bet. Small bodies can get captured, they can be under-resourced, they can develop groupthink, and frankly they can just miss things. Whereas if information about, say, what dangerous capabilities models have shown in evaluations, or what safety incidents have occurred internally, is available to independent researchers, journalists, academics, and the broader public, you get a much more robust error-correcting process.

There's also a legitimacy dimension. The decisions being made about AI could affect basically everyone. If society is going to accept either aggressive regulation or, alternatively, a decision to keep racing ahead, I think people deserve to understand the basis for that. A world where a handful of people at companies and a handful of people in government know that things are getting scary, and everyone else is in the dark, seems both less fair and less stable. You'd expect a big backlash or loss of trust if it came out later.

And practically, transparency is one of the few policy interventions that I think is robustly good across a lot of different worldviews. If you think AI risk is overblown, transparency helps you show that. If you think it's serious, transparency helps you make the case. It doesn't require us to agree in advance on exactly how dangerous things are; it just lets the evidence come out and lets the debate happen in the open.

Now, I don't think literally everything should be public. There are real cases, like specific details of how to elicit dangerous bioweapons uplift or model weights themselves, where you want restrictions. But the default should lean toward openness about what's happening, what's been observed, and what the companies are planning, with narrow carve-outs, rather than defaulting to secrecy with a small trusted group.

r001.rationale: The response describes deep uncertainty about AI capabilities, warning signs, and policy, but does not say safety research is too unsettled for a fixed government checklist.

r002.rationale: It says the relevant unknowns are uncertain, but does not state that the information needed to assess AI safety will likely change over time.

r003.rationale: It supports broad public scrutiny and debate about evidence, but does not say an external scientific conversation should determine what evidence triggers alarm.

r004.rationale: It says small government bodies may be captured, under-resourced, or miss things, but does not clearly connect exclusive routing to delayed interpretation.

r005.rationale: It argues for public discussion and legitimacy, but does not connect a society-wide conversation to sounding an alarm about an intelligence explosion.

r006.rationale: The response does not mention Joe Biden’s debate performance or use it as an analogy for broad deliberation enabling a consequential decision.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a couple of things going on for me here. The first is just a basic epistemic point: I don't think we actually know yet what the most important risks from AI are going to look like, or what the right interventions are. We have theories, we have some empirical work, but this is a field where the frontier is moving very fast and where a lot of the people who've thought hardest about it still disagree with each other quite a bit. And in that situation, I think you want as many eyes on the problem as you can get. You want academics, independent researchers, journalists, people at other labs, people outside the field entirely, all able to look at the evidence and poke at it and say "wait, this doesn't add up" or "you're missing this failure mode." A small government body, however well-intentioned and however talented, is just going to have a narrower set of perspectives and a narrower set of incentives, and it's going to be more prone to groupthink or to getting captured by whichever framing happened to be dominant when it was set up.

The second thing is about trust and legitimacy. If decisions about how to govern these systems are being made behind closed doors based on information the public can't see, then even if those decisions are good, people have no way to verify that. And I think that's corrosive. It makes it very easy for the whole project of AI safety to look like, you know, a handful of insiders deciding the future for everyone else. Whereas if the evidence is out there, if the evals are published, if the incident reports are public, then people can actually check the work, and the policies that come out of that process have a much stronger claim to being legitimate.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I don't think everything should be public. There are real cases, things like specific details of bio or cyber capabilities, or certain kinds of model weights, where broad disclosure genuinely makes the world more dangerous. So I'm not an absolutist about this. But I think the default should be openness, and secrecy should be the thing that has to justify itself case by case, rather than the other way around. My worry is that if you start from the premise that this information is too sensitive for the public, you end up classifying a lot of stuff that really didn't need to be classified, and you lose all the error-correction benefits of having a broad community engaged with the actual evidence. Historically, I think a lot of the progress we've made in understanding these systems has come from exactly that kind of open, somewhat messy, distributed scrutiny, and I'd be nervous about giving that up.

r001.rationale: The response says AI risks and interventions remain uncertain and that broader scrutiny is valuable, but it does not state that the research cannot be reduced to a fixed government checklist.

r002.rationale: It says the AI frontier is moving fast, but does not clearly state that the information needed to assess safety will change over time.

r003.rationale: It describes external scrutiny as useful for challenging evidence and finding failure modes, but does not say that this conversation should determine what evidence triggers alarm.

r004.rationale: It argues that a small government body would have narrower perspectives and be more prone to groupthink or capture, but does not address whether routing evidence through it would impede timely interpretation.

r005.rationale: The response does not discuss an intelligence explosion or say that sounding an effective alarm would require society-wide conversation.

r006.rationale: The response does not mention Joe Biden’s debate performance or use it to illustrate a consequential decision enabled by broad public deliberation.

astra-6.text:
I think a small government body can play an important role, but I wouldn’t want it to be the only place where these questions get examined. There’s a lot of uncertainty about what advanced AI systems will be able to do, what risks they pose, and which safeguards will actually work. If the evidence and assumptions are available for public scrutiny, more people can challenge them, identify mistakes, and propose better approaches.

There’s also an accountability issue. These decisions could affect everybody, so people should have some ability to understand why they’re being made and contest the reasoning. A small group might have expertise, but that doesn’t mean it has all the relevant perspectives or the right incentives.

That doesn’t mean publishing every technical detail. Some information could make it easier to cause harm. But I’d distinguish protecting those details from keeping the broader evidence about safety, and the reasoning behind policy decisions, secret.

r005.rationale: The response does not discuss sounding an alarm about an intelligence explosion or the need for society-wide deliberation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that we don’t know who’s going to notice the crucial flaw in an argument or come up with a better solution. AI safety involves a lot of uncertainty, and if you restrict the relevant information to a small government body, you’re putting a lot of weight on that group’s judgment. Public scrutiny lets people with different expertise challenge assumptions, check the evidence, and point out things that insiders might miss.

There’s also an accountability issue. Decisions about AI could affect everyone, so people should be able to understand and challenge the reasoning behind those decisions. That doesn’t mean every technical detail should be public—some information could enable dangerous capabilities or help someone bypass safeguards. But I’d want a specific reason for keeping something secret, rather than treating secrecy as the default.
